stops.note: a Celtic word for a wagon; Caesar's Gallic War describes the Helvetii gathering carri (baggage carts) for their migration in 58 BC
Romans borrowed the Gaulish word for a four-wheeled baggage wagon; it is also the root of 'carry', 'chariot' and 'career'
the Norman dialect kept the hard k- (central French has char) and brought the word to England after 1066
meant any wheeled vehicle or chariot; it was applied to railway carriages in the US from the 1830s and to motor cars from the 1890s

current_meaning: a road vehicle with an engine, four wheels and seats for a few people
